stem: A page renders `<Image src={user.avatarUrl} alt="" />` for a remote avatar. Next.js refuses to render it until `width` and `height` are added. What are those two props actually for?

options.text: They give the aspect ratio, so space is reserved and layout shift avoided
options.why: Correct: they describe intrinsic size; CSS still decides the rendered size.

options.text: They set the exact rendered size of the image in CSS pixels on every screen
options.why: Rendered size is controlled by CSS; the props only describe the intrinsic size.

options.text: They tell the optimizer to crop the source file to exactly those dimensions
options.why: The optimizer resizes to srcset widths; it does not crop to width and height.

options.text: They are only used to build the `alt` text that screen readers announce
options.why: Alt text comes from the `alt` prop alone; width and height play no part in it.

explanation: The docs describe `width` and `height` as the intrinsic size, used to infer the aspect ratio so the browser can reserve space before the file arrives, which prevents Cumulative Layout Shift. They are required unless the image is statically imported or uses `fill`.
reference: Next.js docs: Image Component (width and height)

stem: With `next/font/google`, each visitor's browser downloads the font files from Google's servers when the page loads.

options.text: True
options.why: Next.js downloads the CSS and font files at build time and self-hosts them with your static assets.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: no requests are sent to Google by the browser; the fonts are served from your own deployment.

explanation: `next/font` self-hosts every font. For Google Fonts the CSS and files are fetched at build time and served from the same origin as your other static assets, so the browser never contacts Google. That also removes a third-party connection from the critical path.

stem: You render `<Image src="/team.jpg" alt="Team" width={800} height={533} />` near the bottom of a long page and pass no other props. When does the browser start fetching it?

options.text: Immediately, because every next/image is preloaded in the document head
options.why: Only images with `preload` get a `<link>` in the head; the default is `preload={false}`.

options.text: When it nears the viewport, because the default is `loading="lazy"`
options.why: Correct: next/image defaults to native lazy loading.

options.text: Only after hydration finishes, because images are client-rendered
options.why: The `` is in the server HTML; lazy loading is native browser behaviour.

options.text: Never, until a `placeholder` prop is supplied to trigger loading
options.why: Placeholders are optional; the default `placeholder` is "empty".

explanation: The `loading` prop defaults to `lazy`, which defers the request until the image is within a browser-calculated distance of the viewport. Use `loading="eager"`, `fetchPriority="high"` or `preload` only for images that must appear immediately, such as the LCP hero.

stem: You add `<Script src="https://example.com/widget.js" />` to a page without a `strategy` prop. Which strategy does `next/script` use? Type the strategy name.
explanation: `afterInteractive` is the default: the script is injected client-side and loads after some or all of the page has hydrated. The other strategies are `beforeInteractive`, `lazyOnload` and the experimental `worker`.

stem: A team upgrades to Next.js 16 and keeps the scripts `"dev": "next dev"` and `"build": "next build"`. Which bundler do they get?

options.text: Webpack for both, unless they pass `--turbopack` to each command
options.why: Before 16 you opted in with `--turbopack`; in 16 Turbopack is the default.

options.text: Turbopack for `next dev` but Webpack for `next build`
options.why: Next.js 16 made Turbopack the default for production builds as well.

options.text: Turbopack for both `next dev` and `next build`
options.why: Correct: Turbopack is stable and the default for both commands.

options.text: Whichever bundler the `bundler` field in package.json names
options.why: There is no such field; you opt out per command with `--webpack`.

explanation: Starting with Next.js 16, Turbopack is stable and used by default by both `next dev` and `next build`. To keep Webpack you pass `--webpack`. A build that finds a custom `webpack` config fails rather than silently ignoring it.
reference: Next.js docs: Upgrading to Version 16 (Turbopack by default)

stem: Match each `next/script` strategy with how it loads.

options.text: `beforeInteractive`
options.why: Fetched early from the server HTML.

options.text: `afterInteractive`
options.why: The default strategy.

options.text: `lazyOnload`
options.why: Waits for idle time.

options.text: `worker`
options.why: Experimental Partytown offloading.

prompts.text: Injected into the initial HTML and fetched before any Next.js code; must be in the root layout
Injected client-side and loaded after some hydration has happened
Loaded during browser idle time, after the page's other resources
Offloaded to a web worker; experimental and Pages Router only

explanation: Choose the latest strategy a script can tolerate. Only scripts every page needs before hydration (bot detectors, consent managers) justify `beforeInteractive`. Most analytics fit `afterInteractive`, chat widgets and social embeds fit `lazyOnload`, and `worker` is still experimental and does not work in the App Router.

stem: Where can a `favicon.ico` file live in the App Router so that Next.js picks it up through the file convention?

options.text: In any route segment, where it overrides the icon for that subtree
options.why: `icon` and `apple-icon` can be nested, but `favicon` cannot.

options.text: Only at the top level of the `app/` directory
options.why: Correct: the favicon file convention is limited to the root of `app/`.

options.text: Only in `public/`, because metadata files must be static assets
options.why: The App Router reads `app/favicon.ico` as a metadata file convention.

options.text: In `app/` or any layout folder, the deepest one winning
options.why: Nesting works for `opengraph-image` and `icon`, not for `favicon`.

explanation: The `favicon` convention accepts only `.ico` files and only at the top level of `app/`. For per-section icons use the `icon` or `apple-icon` conventions, which can be placed in nested segments.
reference: Next.js docs: favicon, icon, and apple-icon

stem: In which two cases can you omit `width` and `height` on `next/image`? (Choose two.)

options.text: The `src` is a static import such as `import hero from "./hero.png"`
options.why: Correct: Next.js reads the dimensions from the file at build time.

options.text: The image uses the `fill` prop inside a positioned parent
options.why: Correct: `fill` sizes the image to its parent instead.

options.text: The image has a `sizes` prop describing its rendered width
options.why: `sizes` guides srcset selection; it does not give the aspect ratio.

options.text: The image has `preload` set because it is the LCP element
options.why: Preloading changes when the image is fetched, not its dimensions.

options.text: The image is remote and listed in `images.remotePatterns`
options.why: Remote images still need explicit dimensions (or `fill`).

explanation: Dimensions are required unless they can be inferred (a static import) or are irrelevant because the image fills its parent (`fill`, with a parent positioned `relative`, `fixed` or `absolute`). For remote images of unknown size, the docs recommend `fill`.
reference: Next.js docs: Image Component (width and height)

stem: After upgrading to Next.js 16 you see that `priority` is deprecated on your hero `<Image>`. Which prop replaces it?

options.text: `eager`, a boolean that disables lazy loading
options.why: There is no `eager` boolean; laziness is controlled by `loading="eager"`.

options.text: `preload`, which adds a head `<link>` for the image
options.why: Correct: Next.js 16 deprecated `priority` in favour of `preload`.

options.text: `fetchPriority`, which Next.js 16 added as a new prop
options.why: `fetchPriority` is a native attribute passed through, not the replacement.

options.text: `critical`, which also inlines the image as base64
options.why: There is no `critical` prop, and next/image never inlines the full image.

explanation: Next.js 16 deprecated `priority` and introduced `preload` to make the behaviour clearer: `preload` inserts a `<link rel="preload">` in the head. The docs add that in most cases `loading="eager"` or `fetchPriority="high"` is the better choice, and that `preload` shouldn't be combined with them.

stem:
With the default image config, what `srcset` does Next.js generate for this image?

```tsx
<Image src="/p.jpg" alt="" width={500} height={300} />
```

options.text: `500w` and `1000w` width descriptors matching the props
options.why: Next.js only emits widths from its configured size list, never arbitrary ones.

options.text: Every device size from `640w` to `3840w` with `sizes="100vw"`
options.why: The full width list is used with `sizes` or `fill`, not for a fixed width.

options.text: `640 1x` and `1080 2x` density descriptors
options.why: Correct: 500 rounds up to 640 and 1000 rounds up to 1080 in the size list.

options.text: `384 1x` and `750 2x`, rounding each density down
options.why: Next.js rounds up so the image is never upscaled, never down.

explanation: Without `sizes`, Next.js builds a limited 1x/2x `srcset` for a fixed-size image. The width list is the default `imageSizes` [32, 48, 64, 96, 128, 256, 384] plus `deviceSizes` [640, 750, 828, 1080, 1200, 1920, 2048, 3840]. For 1x it picks the smallest entry ≥ 500, which is 640; for 2x the smallest ≥ 1000, which is 1080. Running `getImageProps` with Next.js 16.3 confirms `…w=640… 1x, …w=1080… 2x`.
reference: Next.js docs: Image Component (sizes, deviceSizes, imageSizes)

stem: A product card uses `<Image fill src={p.photo} alt={p.name} />` with no `sizes` prop. What does Next.js output?

options.text: `sizes="100vw"` plus a device-size srcset, 640w to 3840w
options.why: Correct: the browser is told the image is viewport-wide.

options.text: A 1x/2x srcset based on the size of the parent element
options.why: Next.js can't know the parent's size at render time, so it can't do this.

options.text: No srcset at all, just a single `src` at the original resolution
options.why: A srcset is still generated; it is just tuned for full-width images.

options.text: A build error, because `fill` images must always declare `sizes`
options.why: `sizes` is strongly advised for `fill`, but it is not required.

explanation: For `fill` without `sizes`, Next.js sets `sizes="100vw"` and lists only `deviceSizes` (640w to 3840w), as running `getImageProps` with Next.js 16.3 shows. The browser then assumes the image spans the viewport, so a card that is really 300px wide downloads a far larger file. Always pass `sizes` to `fill` images that are narrower than the viewport.

stem: A Next.js 16 app has no `images.qualities` setting. A designer adds `quality={90}` to a hero image. What happens?

options.text: The image is served at quality 90, the value the prop requested
options.why: Next.js 16 only allows `[75]` by default, so 90 is not permitted.

options.text: It is served at 75, the closest allowed value, with a dev warning
options.why: Correct: values outside `qualities` are coerced to the nearest allowed one.

options.text: The page fails to render with an error about the quality value
options.why: The component coerces the value; only a hand-built API URL gets a 400.

options.text: It is served at 100, because any value above 75 is rounded up
options.why: Coercion picks the closest allowed value, and only 75 is allowed.

explanation: In Next.js 16 `images.qualities` defaults to `[75]` instead of allowing every value. A `quality` prop outside the list is coerced to the closest allowed entry, and development logs a warning suggesting you add it, for example `[75, 90]`. Running `getImageProps` with `quality: 90` returns `q=75` URLs and prints that warning.

stem: A root layout sets `title: { template: '%s | Acme' }`. Which other property of `title` must it also set when it defines a template? Type the property name.
explanation: The docs state that `title.default` is required when you add `title.template`. It is the fallback title for child segments that set no title of their own, and the template only has an effect if the route has a `title` or a `title.default`.

stem: A layout sets `openGraph: { images: '/og.png' }` and nothing else URL-related. What happens?

options.text: Next.js emits `og:image` as `/og.png`, a relative URL crawlers resolve
options.why: A relative URL here is not allowed without a base, and many crawlers would fail on it.

options.text: Next.js prefixes it with the request's Host header at runtime
options.why: Composition uses `metadataBase`, not the incoming request.

options.text: The build fails, because a relative URL needs `metadataBase`
options.why: Correct: relative URL fields without `metadataBase` cause a build error.

options.text: The image is silently dropped from the rendered metadata
options.why: It isn't dropped; the docs say a missing base is a build error.

explanation: Fields such as `openGraph.images` need fully qualified URLs. `metadataBase` (usually set once in the root layout, e.g. `new URL('https://acme.com')`) lets the current segment and its children use relative paths, which are composed into absolute URLs. Per the docs, using a relative path without configuring `metadataBase` is a build error.

stem: Which two statements about `next/font` are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Each call to a font function hosts a separate instance, so define each font once and import it
options.why: Correct: the docs recommend a shared font definitions file.

options.text: A variable Google font such as `Inter` can be loaded without a `weight` option
options.why: Correct: `weight` is only required for non-variable fonts.

options.text: A font called in `app/blog/page.tsx` is preloaded on every route
options.why: Fonts called in a page are preloaded only on that page's route.

options.text: The default `display` value is `block`, hiding text until the font loads
options.why: The default is `swap`.

options.text: `adjustFontFallback` is off by default and must be enabled to reduce CLS
options.why: For Google fonts it defaults to `true`, adding a size-adjusted fallback.

explanation: Every font function call creates its own hosted instance, so calling `Inter()` in five files duplicates work; export it from one `fonts.ts`. Variable fonts include the weight axis, so `weight` is optional. `display` defaults to `swap`, `preload` to `true`, and `adjustFontFallback` (Google) to `true`, which adds a metrics-matched fallback font to prevent layout shift.

stem:
A Server Component page contains this code, and the build fails:

```tsx
const Map = dynamic(() => import('./map'), { ssr: false })
```

What is the fix?

options.text: Wrap the `dynamic` call in `<Suspense>` so that it can stream
options.why: Suspense doesn't change the rule: `ssr: false` isn't allowed in Server Components.

options.text: Replace `next/dynamic` with `React.lazy`, which supports `ssr: false`
options.why: `React.lazy` has no `ssr` option, and Client Components are still prerendered with it.

options.text: Move the `dynamic(..., { ssr: false })` call into a Client Component
options.why: Correct: the docs say to move it into a Client Component.

options.text: Add `export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'` to the page
options.why: That segment option controls rendering, not whether `ssr: false` is allowed.

explanation: `ssr: false` is not supported in Server Components; Next.js errors with "`ssr: false` is not allowed with `next/dynamic` in Server Components. Please move it into a Client Component." The usual pattern is a small `'use client'` wrapper that calls `dynamic(() => import('./map'), { ssr: false })`, rendered from the server page.

stem: You want to send Core Web Vitals to your analytics with `useReportWebVitals`. Where should the hook live in an App Router app?

options.text: Directly in `app/layout.tsx`, after marking the root layout `'use client'`
options.why: That turns the whole layout and its imports into client code just for one hook.

options.text: In a small `'use client'` component that the root layout renders
options.why: Correct: it confines the client boundary to the reporting component.

options.text: In `instrumentation.ts`, which runs once when the server boots
options.why: Web Vitals are measured in the browser, so the hook must run client-side.

options.text: In every page file, so each route reports its own metrics
options.why: One component in the root layout covers every route.

explanation: `useReportWebVitals` from `next/web-vitals` needs `'use client'`. The docs recommend a separate component (for example `app/_components/web-vitals.js`) that the root layout imports, which keeps the client boundary as small as possible. Keep the callback reference stable so metrics aren't reported twice.

stem: On a first page load, put these `next/script` strategies in the order their scripts start loading, earliest first.

options.text: `lazyOnload`
options.why: Loads during idle time.

options.text: `beforeInteractive`
options.why: Loads before Next.js code.

options.text: `afterInteractive`
options.why: Loads after hydration starts.

explanation: `beforeInteractive` scripts are in the server HTML and fetched before any first-party Next.js modules, though they don't block hydration. `afterInteractive` scripts are injected client-side once some hydration has happened. `lazyOnload` waits for browser idle time, after the page's other resources have loaded.

stem: In Next.js 16, the recommended place to set `themeColor` is the `metadata` export of a layout or page.

options.text: True
options.why: `themeColor` in `metadata` has been deprecated since Next.js 14.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: set it in the `viewport` export or `generateViewport` instead.

explanation: `themeColor` and `colorScheme` moved out of `metadata` in Next.js 14 and are deprecated there. Use `export const viewport = { themeColor: 'black' }` or `generateViewport`. You can't export both `viewport` and `generateViewport` from the same segment.

stem: A grid card is 300px wide on a 1440px-wide desktop with a device pixel ratio of 1. The card uses `<Image fill src="/p.jpg" alt="" />` with no `sizes`. Which candidate does the browser download from the default srcset?

options.text: `384w`, the smallest candidate at least 300px wide
options.why: 384w isn't in the srcset: without `sizes` only device sizes are listed.

options.text: `640w`, the smallest device size in the srcset
options.why: The browser looks for a candidate covering 1440px, not the smallest one.

options.text: `1920w`, because the browser assumes `100vw`, so 1440px
options.why: Correct: 1440 × 1 = 1440, and the smallest candidate ≥ 1440 is 1920w.

options.text: `3840w`, because `fill` always requests the largest width
options.why: Selection follows `sizes` and DPR, not a rule to pick the maximum.

explanation: Without `sizes`, Next.js emits `sizes="100vw"` and the device-size srcset (640w … 3840w). The browser computes the slot as 100vw = 1440 CSS px × DPR 1 = 1440 device px, then picks the smallest candidate covering it: 1920w. That is over six times the width the 300px card needs. With `sizes="300px"`, the srcset adds the image sizes 384w and above and the browser picks 384w.

stem: An image uses `sizes="(max-width: 768px) 100vw, 33vw"` with the default image config. On a phone with a 390px-wide viewport and a device pixel ratio of 3, which candidate does the browser pick?

options.text: `384w`, because the slot is 390px wide
options.why: The slot must be multiplied by the pixel ratio: 390 × 3 = 1170.

options.text: `1080w`, the widest candidate smaller than 1170
options.why: Browsers choose a candidate at least as wide as needed, never a narrower one.

options.text: `1200w`, the smallest width covering 390 × 3 = 1170
options.why: Correct: the 768px query matches, so 100vw = 390px and 390 × 3 = 1170.

options.text: `3840w`, because a DPR above 2 requests the largest file
options.why: There is no such rule; the browser does width arithmetic.

explanation: The viewport is under 768px, so the slot is 100vw = 390 CSS px. Multiplying by DPR 3 gives 1170 device px. The srcset (default sizes) is 256, 384, 640, 750, 828, 1080, 1200, 1920, 2048 and 3840w, and the smallest width ≥ 1170 is 1200w. Next.js 16.3's `getImageProps` produced exactly that srcset for this `sizes` value.

stem: The same image (`sizes="(max-width: 768px) 100vw, 33vw"`, default config) is viewed on a 1440px-wide laptop with a device pixel ratio of 2. Which candidate is chosen?

options.text: `1080w`, since 33vw is 475.2px and × 2 is about 950px
options.why: Correct: the smallest candidate ≥ 950.4 is 1080w.

options.text: `1920w`, because the laptop viewport itself is 1440px
options.why: The slot is 33vw, not the full viewport, once the media query fails.

options.text: `640w`, since a 33vw slot is roughly 475px
options.why: The DPR of 2 doubles the needed width to about 950px.

options.text: `2048w`, the next size above double the viewport
options.why: That would fit a 100vw slot at DPR 1.4, not this one.

explanation: At 1440px the `(max-width: 768px)` condition is false, so the slot is 33vw = 0.33 × 1440 = 475.2 CSS px. At DPR 2 that is 950.4 device px, and the smallest candidate ≥ 950.4 is 1080w. Getting `sizes` right saves a lot here: with no `sizes`, the browser would assume 100vw and fetch 2880 device px, the 3840w file.

stem: A `title.template` of `'%s | Blog'` set in `app/blog/layout.tsx` is applied to the title `'All posts'` exported from `app/blog/page.tsx`.

options.text: True
options.why: The template only applies to child route segments, not to a page in the same segment.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: the docs say a layout's template doesn't apply to a page in the same route segment.

explanation: Per the docs, `title.template` applies to child route segments and not to the segment it is defined in. A template in `app/blog/layout.js` doesn't apply to a `title` defined in `app/blog/page.js`, which is the same route segment, but it does apply to `app/blog/[slug]/page.js`. A template in a `page.js` has no effect at all, because a page is always the terminating segment.

options.text: og:title "Blog" plus the root's og:description and og:image
options.why: That would need a deep merge; Next.js merges metadata shallowly.

options.text: Only og:title "Blog"; the root's description and image are lost
options.why: Correct: the page's `openGraph` object replaces the root's whole object.

options.text: og:title "Acme", because the root layout is evaluated last
options.why: Metadata is evaluated root first, so the page's value wins.

options.text: Both og:title tags, "Acme" and then "Blog", in that order
options.why: Duplicate keys are replaced, not emitted twice.

explanation: Metadata objects from the segments of a route are evaluated from the root down and merged shallowly, and duplicate keys are replaced. Because the page sets `openGraph`, the entire root `openGraph` object, including `description` and `images`, is overwritten. To share nested fields, export a shared object (e.g. `sharedOg`) and spread it: `openGraph: { ...sharedOg, title: 'Blog' }`.

options.text: `Sign in to Acme | Acme`, because every child title uses the template
options.why: `absolute` exists to opt out of parent templates.

options.text: `Sign in to Acme`
options.why: Correct: `title.absolute` ignores templates set in parent segments.

options.text: `Acme`, because a page can't override the layout's default
options.why: Child segments can override the default title.

options.text: `Sign in to Acme | Sign in to Acme`, applied twice
options.why: Templates are applied at most once, and `absolute` skips them.

explanation: In a page, a string `title` augments the closest parent `title.template`, while `title.absolute` sets the title and ignores parent templates. Use it for pages such as login or landing pages where the brand suffix would be redundant.

stem: A page's `generateMetadata` awaits a slow CMS call. Which three statements describe Next.js 16's default behaviour? (Choose three.)

options.text: The initial UI can be sent first; the metadata tags are appended to `<body>` when they resolve
options.why: Correct: this is streaming metadata.

options.text: HTML-limited bots such as `facebookexternalhit` still get the metadata, blocking, in `<head>`
options.why: Correct: Next.js detects them from the User-Agent.

options.text: Setting `htmlLimitedBots: /.*/` in next.config disables streaming metadata
options.why: Correct: every client is then treated as HTML-limited.

options.text: Streamed metadata is invisible to Googlebot, so SEO tags must be static
options.why: Next.js says bots that execute JavaScript, like Googlebot, read it correctly.

options.text: The same `fetch` in `generateMetadata` and in the page runs twice
options.why: `fetch` requests are memoized across generateMetadata, layouts and pages.

explanation: Streaming metadata lets Next.js send the UI without waiting for `generateMetadata`. The resolved tags are appended to `<body>`, which the Next.js docs say JavaScript-executing crawlers such as Googlebot handle correctly. For HTML-limited bots, detected via the User-Agent and configurable with `htmlLimitedBots`, metadata still blocks and lands in `<head>`. Identical `fetch` calls are memoized across `generateMetadata`, layouts, pages and Server Components.

stem: Dev startup is slow. The app imports icons from `lucide-react` and from an in-house barrel package, `@acme/icons`, which re-exports 4,000 modules. What should go in `experimental.optimizePackageImports`?

options.text: Both packages, because neither is optimized unless listed
options.why: `lucide-react` is on the list of packages Next.js optimizes by default.

options.text: Only `@acme/icons`; `lucide-react` is optimized by default
options.why: Correct: listing the in-house barrel is what helps.

options.text: Nothing: Turbopack tree-shakes barrels, so the option is ignored
options.why: The option still applies; it makes Next.js load only the modules you use.

options.text: Only `lucide-react`, because the option rejects private packages
options.why: Any package name can be listed, private or public.

explanation: `optimizePackageImports` makes Next.js load only the modules you actually import from a package with many exports, which speeds up dev and builds. Several popular libraries are optimized by default, including `lucide-react`, `date-fns`, `lodash-es` and `@heroicons/react`, so only the in-house barrel needs listing.

stem: A blog post page is marked `'use client'` so it can syntax-highlight code with a large library and open a share modal. The client bundle is huge. Which two changes reduce the JavaScript shipped? (Choose two.)

options.text: Do the highlighting in a Server Component, since it needs no browser APIs
options.why: Correct: the library then stays on the server and only HTML is sent.

options.text: Lazy-load the modal with `next/dynamic` so its code loads on demand
options.why: Correct: the modal leaves the initial bundle.

options.text: Enable `reactCompiler`, which strips unused libraries from client bundles
options.why: The React Compiler memoizes rendering; it doesn't remove dependencies.

options.text: Add `lucide-react` to `optimizePackageImports` to shrink the highlighter
options.why: Unrelated, and `lucide-react` is already optimized by default.

options.text: Move `'use client'` up into the root layout so code is shared
options.why: That puts even more of the tree into the client bundle.

explanation: The Next.js bundling guide calls out exactly this case: libraries that only turn data into UI, such as highlighters, chart renderers and markdown parsers, can run in Server Components, so none of their code reaches the client. Interaction-only pieces like a modal can be deferred with `next/dynamic` or `React.lazy`. Keep `'use client'` boundaries as low and as small as possible.
reference: Next.js docs: Package Bundling (Heavy client workloads); Lazy Loading

stem: To use a theme hook, a developer adds `'use client'` to the top of `app/layout.tsx`. The root layout also exports `metadata` and imports a heavy analytics SDK. What goes wrong?

options.text: Only the page components become client code; the layout stays a Server Component
options.why: `'use client'` applies to the file it is in, which here is the layout itself.

options.text: The `metadata` export stops working, and the layout's imports ship to the client
options.why: Correct: metadata exports are Server Component only, and the boundary moved up.

options.text: Nothing changes, because the root layout is always forced to render on the server
options.why: There is no such exception for the root layout.

options.text: Every nested page must now also be marked `'use client'`
options.why: Pages passed as `children` can still be Server Components.

explanation: `metadata` and `generateMetadata` are supported only in Server Components, so a client root layout can't export them. `'use client'` also makes the layout and every module it imports, such as the analytics SDK, part of the client bundle. Pages passed in as `children` can remain Server Components. The fix is a small `ThemeProvider` Client Component that wraps `children`, rendered from a server root layout.
reference: Next.js docs: generateMetadata (Server Component only); Package Bundling

stem: The LCP element on a landing page is a full-width hero `<Image fill src={hero} alt="" />`, and LCP is poor. Which two changes help? (Choose two.)

options.text: Mark it `loading="eager"` or `fetchPriority="high"` (or `preload`)
options.why: Correct: the lazy default delays the LCP request.

options.text: Give it an accurate `sizes` value so a smaller file can be chosen
options.why: Correct: smaller bytes arrive sooner on narrow screens.

options.text: Add `placeholder="blur"`, since the blurred preview counts as LCP
options.why: A placeholder improves perceived loading, not the LCP measurement.

options.text: Set `unoptimized` to skip the optimizer's processing delay
options.why: That serves the full original file, which is usually much larger.

options.text: Keep `loading="lazy"` so the browser saves bandwidth
options.why: Lazy loading the LCP image postpones the very request you need first.

explanation: next/image lazy-loads by default, which is wrong for the LCP image, so make it eager or high-priority. The docs list `preload` for the LCP or above-the-fold hero, but suggest `loading="eager"` or `fetchPriority="high"` in most cases. A `fill` hero without `sizes` assumes 100vw, which may be right for a truly full-width hero but wasteful for anything narrower.
reference: Next.js docs: Image Component (preload, loading, sizes)

stem: With the default image config, `<Image src="/a.jpg" alt="" width={300} height={300} />` (no `sizes`) gets a two-entry srcset. What width, in pixels, is the `2x` candidate? Type a number.
explanation: Next.js picks, from imageSizes + deviceSizes (32 … 384, 640 … 3840), the smallest width ≥ 300 for 1x, which is 384, and the smallest ≥ 2 × 300 = 600 for 2x, which is 640. Running Next.js 16.3's `getImageProps` gives `…w=384… 1x, …w=640… 2x`.

stem: A self-hosted app sets `images.formats: ['image/avif', 'image/webp']`, but every optimized image is served as JPEG. The CDN in front of Next.js strips most request headers. What is the likely cause?

options.text: AVIF needs `dangerouslyAllowSVG` before the encoder is enabled
options.why: That flag is about SVG sources and is unrelated to output formats.

options.text: The `formats` array must list `image/jpeg` first as a fallback
options.why: Fallback to the original format happens automatically when nothing matches.

options.text: The CDN drops `Accept`, so Next.js falls back to the original format
options.why: Correct: Next.js picks formats from the request's `Accept` header.

options.text: Next.js only serves AVIF on Vercel, so self-hosted output stays JPEG
options.why: Self-hosted servers can encode AVIF; it's slower but supported.

explanation: Next.js chooses the output format from the browser's `Accept` header: the first configured format that matches wins, and with no match, or for animated images, the original format is used. Behind a proxy or CDN you must forward `Accept`, and the CDN should vary its cache on it. Each format is also cached separately, which roughly doubles storage when both are enabled.

stem: A self-hosted Next.js 16 app replaces `public/banner.jpg` with a new file under the same name. Hours later, `<Image src="/banner.jpg" ... />` still serves the old optimized version. What is the documented way out?

options.text: Call `revalidatePath('/_next/image')` to purge the optimizer cache
options.why: There is no mechanism to invalidate the image optimization cache.

options.text: Change the `src` or delete the `<distDir>/cache/images` folder
options.why: Correct: the docs offer exactly these two options.

options.text: Set `qualities: [76]` so the cache key changes for every image
options.why: Hacky, and it changes every image's quality rather than invalidating cleanly.

options.text: Wait 60 seconds, the default `minimumCacheTTL`
options.why: The Next.js 16 default is 14400 seconds (4 hours), not 60.

explanation: Optimized images are cached for the larger of `minimumCacheTTL` (4 hours by default in Next.js 16) and the upstream `Cache-Control` max-age, and the docs say there is no mechanism to invalidate that cache. Change the `src`, or delete the cached files. Better still, use static imports, which hash the file contents and get an `immutable` Cache-Control.

stem: Match each `images` option in `next.config` with what it controls.

options.text: `remotePatterns`
options.why: External sources allowlist.

options.text: `localPatterns`
options.why: Local sources allowlist.

options.text: `qualities`
options.why: Quality allowlist.

options.text: `minimumCacheTTL`
options.why: Cache lifetime floor.

prompts.text: Which external protocol, host, path and query the optimizer may fetch; anything else gets 400
Which local paths and query strings may be optimized, needed in 16 for a src like `/photo?v=1`
The allowed quality values, `[75]` by default in Next.js 16
The minimum seconds an optimized image stays cached, 14400 (4 hours) by default in 16

explanation: Next.js 16 tightened several image defaults for safety and cost: local images with query strings need a `localPatterns.search` entry, `qualities` defaults to `[75]`, `minimumCacheTTL` rose from 60 seconds to 4 hours, and redirects are capped at 3. `remotePatterns` replaces the deprecated `domains`.
reference: Next.js docs: Upgrading to Version 16 (next/image changes)

stem: `app/(marketing)/page.tsx` imports `./landing.css`, which sets `body { background: black }`. After client-side navigation to `/dashboard`, the dashboard also has a black background. Why?

options.text: CSS imported in a page is inlined into the root layout's chunk at build time
options.why: It isn't moved into the layout; the stylesheet just isn't removed on navigation.

options.text: Stylesheets aren't removed on navigation, so global rules stay active
options.why: Correct: the docs warn this can cause conflicts.

options.text: The dashboard reuses the marketing route's cached RSC payload
options.why: The RSC payload doesn't contain styles; this is about stylesheet lifetime.

options.text: Turbopack orders CSS alphabetically, so landing.css always loads last
options.why: CSS order follows import order, not file names.

explanation: Global CSS can be imported anywhere in `app/`, but Next.js uses React's stylesheet support for Suspense, which currently doesn't remove stylesheets as you navigate. A global rule from one route can therefore leak into routes you visit afterwards. Keep only truly global CSS (resets, Tailwind base) global, and use CSS Modules or Tailwind classes for route- or component-specific styles.

stem:
This file is `app/dashboard/layout.tsx`, a Client Component. Which two problems does it have? (Choose two.)

```tsx
'use client'
import Script from 'next/script'
export default function Layout({ children }) {
  return (<>
    <Script src="https://cdn.example.com/consent.js" strategy="beforeInteractive"
      onLoad={() => window.Consent.init()} />
    {children}
  </>)
}
```

options.text: `beforeInteractive` scripts must be placed in a root layout
options.why: Correct: a nested dashboard layout is not a root layout.

options.text: `onLoad` can't be combined with `beforeInteractive`; use `onReady`
options.why: Correct: the docs call out this restriction explicitly.

options.text: `next/script` can't be rendered from Client Components at all
options.why: It can; `onLoad`, `onReady` and `onError` even require a Client Component.

options.text: `beforeInteractive` blocks hydration until the script finishes
options.why: It is fetched early, but its execution doesn't block hydration.

options.text: External scripts need an `id` prop, or Next.js loads them twice
options.why: The `id` is required for inline scripts, not for ones with `src`.

explanation: `beforeInteractive` is for site-wide critical scripts, so it must live in a root layout such as `app/layout.tsx` or `app/[locale]/layout.tsx`, and it is always injected into `<head>`. `onLoad` doesn't work with `beforeInteractive`; the docs suggest `onReady`. The event handlers do require a Client Component, so that part is right.

stem: `app/[locale]/layout.tsx` is the root layout and loads a script with `strategy="beforeInteractive"` that reads the locale from the URL once. A user switches from `/en` to `/fi` with a client-side `<Link>`. What happens to the script?

options.text: It runs again, because `[locale]` changing remounts the root layout
options.why: The docs say a navigation that only changes a root param doesn't re-run it.

options.text: It doesn't run again; it still holds the `en` value from first load
options.why: Correct: beforeInteractive scripts run once per document load.

options.text: It runs again only if the script tag has a `key` that includes the locale
options.why: Keys don't re-execute beforeInteractive scripts on client navigation.

options.text: The navigation turns into a full reload so the script can run again
options.why: Client navigation stays client-side; nothing forces a reload.

explanation: `beforeInteractive` scripts run once per document load. Per the docs, a client-side navigation doesn't run them again, including one that only changes a root param such as `/en` to `/fi`, because the root layout stays the same. Logic that must follow the locale should read it on each navigation in React, or the switch should be a full document navigation.

stem: With the default image config, `<Image fill sizes="50vw" src="/p.jpg" alt="" />` gets a srcset of device sizes plus some of the smaller `imageSizes`. Which `imageSizes` entries appear?

options.text: None, because `imageSizes` is only used for fixed-width images
options.why: It's the reverse: `imageSizes` is only used when a `sizes` prop is present.

options.text: All seven, from `32w` up to `384w`
options.why: Widths far below any plausible 50vw slot are filtered out.

options.text: Only `384w`; Next.js keeps sizes ≥ 0.5 × 640 = 320
options.why: Correct: the smallest vw percentage times the smallest device size sets the cut-off.

options.text: `256w` and `384w`, everything above a quarter of 640
options.why: For 50vw the cut-off is 320, so 256 is dropped.

explanation: Running `getImageProps` with Next.js 16.3 for `sizes="50vw"` gives 384w, 640w, 750w, 828w, 1080w, 1200w, 1920w, 2048w and 3840w. Next.js parses the smallest `vw` value in `sizes` (50%) and drops any width below that fraction of the smallest device size: 0.5 × 640 = 320, so 384 is the only image size kept. With `33vw` the cut-off is about 211, so 256w and 384w both appear.
reference: Next.js docs: Image Component (imageSizes); verified with next/image getImageProps

stem: next.config sets `images.qualities: [50, 75, 100]`. A component renders `<Image quality={80} ... />`, and a scraper requests `/_next/image?url=%2Fa.jpg&w=640&q=80` directly. What does each get?

options.text: Both are served at quality 80, a value between two allowed entries
options.why: Values outside the list are never served as requested.

options.text: The prop is coerced to 75; the direct URL gets `400 Bad Request`
options.why: Correct: the prop is coerced, but the REST API rejects unlisted values.

options.text: Both are coerced to 75, the closest allowed value
options.why: Only the component coerces; the API answers a mismatch with 400.

options.text: The component errors in production; the direct URL is served at 100
options.why: There is no production error, and the API never rounds up silently.

explanation: The `qualities` allowlist protects the optimizer from being used to generate unlimited variants. When the prop doesn't match, Next.js uses the closest allowed value: 80 becomes 75, with a dev warning. A direct request to the Image Optimization API with an unlisted quality gets a 400 Bad Request.

stem: `images.remotePatterns` allows only `https://cdn.partner.com/img/**`, and nothing else. A partner image URL starts returning a 302 redirect to `https://random-host.example/x.jpg`. What does the default Next.js 16 optimizer do?

options.text: Rejects the image with a 400 because the redirect target isn't allowed
options.why: Redirect targets aren't validated against remotePatterns again.

options.text: Follows it (up to 3 redirects) without re-checking remotePatterns
options.why: Correct: set `maximumRedirects: 0` if this is unacceptable.

options.text: Returns the 302 to the browser, which fetches the target itself
options.why: The optimizer follows the redirect server-side and returns the optimized image.

options.text: Follows any number of redirects until it reaches an image
options.why: Next.js 16 changed the default from unlimited to 3.

explanation: The docs say allowed remote patterns that respond with a redirect are followed without validating `remotePatterns` again on the redirect location, up to `maximumRedirects` (default 3 since Next.js 16, previously unlimited). If a partner could be compromised or a URL hijacked, set `maximumRedirects: 0`. Local IPs are blocked by default (`dangerouslyAllowLocalIP: false`).

stem: An `opengraph-image.tsx` returns an `ImageResponse` whose JSX uses `display: 'grid'` for layout and loads a `.woff2` brand font. The cards render with broken layout and the default font. Which explains both problems?

options.text: ImageResponse renders in a browser, so grid needs a polyfill and woff2 a MIME type
options.why: It renders to an image without a browser, supporting only a subset of CSS.

options.text: Only flexbox and a CSS subset are supported, and fonts must be ttf, otf or woff
options.why: Correct: grid isn't supported and woff2 isn't a supported font format.

options.text: Both stem from the 500KB bundle limit, which drops grid styles and fonts
options.why: The size limit is real, but it isn't why grid and woff2 fail.

options.text: OG images must be static files, so the JSX is ignored and a fallback is used
options.why: Code-generated `opengraph-image` routes are fully supported.

explanation: The `ImageResponse` docs list the limits: only flexbox and a subset of CSS properties (`display: grid` won't work), a 500KB bundle limit covering JSX, CSS, fonts and images, and only `ttf`, `otf` and `woff` fonts, with `ttf`/`otf` parsing fastest. Convert the font, and build layouts with flexbox and absolute positioning.

options.text: OG image routes no longer receive `params`; use `useParams()` instead
options.why: They still receive params; hooks can't be used in image routes.

options.text: In 16 `params` is a Promise, so `params.slug` is undefined
options.why: Correct: write `const { slug } = await params`.

options.text: The image is prerendered at build, so dynamic segments are always empty
options.why: It can still use params; static generation doesn't blank them.

options.text: `ImageResponse` escapes JSX text, so the name must be passed as a prop
options.why: JSX text renders normally; the value is undefined before it gets there.

explanation: Next.js 16 made the props of image-generating functions (`opengraph-image`, `twitter-image`, `icon`, `apple-icon`) asynchronous: `params`, and `id` when using `generateImageMetadata`, are Promises. Reading `.slug` off a Promise gives `undefined`. `generateImageMetadata` itself still receives synchronous `params`.
reference: Next.js docs: Upgrading to Version 16 (async params for icon and OG image)

stem: Where `next/font` preloads a font depends on the file that calls the font function. Which three statements are true? (Choose three.)

options.text: Called in `app/blog/page.tsx`, it is preloaded only on that page's route
options.why: Correct: a page preloads its fonts on its own route.

options.text: Called in `app/blog/layout.tsx`, it is preloaded on all routes that layout wraps
options.why: Correct: layouts preload for every route under them.

options.text: Called in the root layout, it is preloaded on every route
options.why: Correct: the root layout wraps all routes.

options.text: Any call anywhere makes the font globally preloaded on all routes
options.why: Preloading is scoped to the routes of the calling file.

options.text: Omitting `subsets` while `preload` is true fails the build
options.why: It produces a warning, not a build failure.

explanation: A font isn't globally preloaded just because it is defined. It is preloaded on the routes related to the calling file: a page preloads on its route, a layout on every route it wraps, and the root layout on all routes. Forgetting `subsets` with `preload: true` only logs a warning, but you should still specify subsets so the right files are preloaded.
reference: Next.js docs: Font Module (Preloading, Specifying a subset)

stem: Using Cache Components, a layout's `generateMetadata` starts with `'use cache'` and returns `{ metadataBase: new URL(process.env.SITE_URL!), ... }`. It now fails. What change does the documentation prescribe?

options.text: Remove `metadataBase`; with `'use cache'` relative URLs resolve on their own
options.why: Relative URL fields still need a base to become absolute.

options.text: Move `metadataBase` to `next.config`, where cached metadata reads it
options.why: There is no `metadataBase` option in next.config.

options.text: Return it as a string, such as `url.toString()`, not a `URL` instance
options.why: Correct: cached return values must be serializable, and `URL` isn't.

options.text: Wrap the `URL` in `JSON.stringify` so the cache stores its fields
options.why: Stringifying a URL with JSON gives a quoted string, not a usable base.

explanation: Values returned from a `'use cache'` function must be serializable, and `URL` instances aren't supported by Cache Functions. The `generateMetadata` docs say to return values such as `metadataBase` as strings, for example `url.toString()`. Next.js still composes relative fields with that base.
reference: Next.js docs: generateMetadata (metadataBase with use cache)

stem: For the route `/blog/hello`, put these metadata sources in the order Next.js evaluates them, first to last.

options.text: `app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx`
options.why: The page.

options.text: `app/layout.tsx`
options.why: The root layout.

options.text: `app/blog/[slug]/layout.tsx`
options.why: The slug layout.

options.text: `app/blog/layout.tsx`
options.why: The blog layout.

explanation: Metadata is evaluated from the root segment down to the segment closest to the final `page.js`, then merged shallowly. Because later segments replace duplicate keys, the page has the last word on any field it sets.
